subject: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter

messages.author: d16378cf7bf5eca2
messages.subject: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
parts:
Dear Mike,

I'm predicting intertidal mussel body temperatures using microclimate(). 

Gehman & Harley (2019; https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.2683) have estimated the spectral reflectance curve (between 300 and 1100 nm) of the shells of two types of mussels (see Fig 4A in their paper).

How can I integrate it in NicheMapR? Can the REFL parameter take multiple values to take into account varying reflectances over a range of wavelengths?

Thanks for your help!

Best,

Jonathan

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
parts:
Dear Jonathan,

The REFL parameter is the 'reflectivity' of an object, specifically for the solar spectrum. A reflectance curve tells you how energy is absorbed across different wavelengths. If you know the intensity of energy across different wavelengths for incoming radiation then you can use that to get an appropriately weighted mean reflectivity of the object. As you would have seen in that paper you referred to, "The absorption spectrum (350–1100 nm) was multiplied by the power spectrum of incoming solar radiation measured at the Hopkins Marine Station (data courtesy of M. Denny; see Denny and Harley 2006 for details). The resulting energy absorbed is expressed in Wm−2." The reported the total energy absorbed but if they divided that by the total incoming energy and converted to a percentage, they would have the REFL parameter required by the model.

All the best,
Mike

messages.author: d16378cf7bf5eca2
messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
parts:
Thank you for the clarifications Mike!

So, I can either use their estimations of absorbed energy and the total irradiance (using ASTM G-173 standard irradiance spectrum) within their range of wavelengths (code chunk 1 below) or calculate it directly from spectral reflectance curves (code chunk 2). Correct?

### 1. calculation of REFL using absorbed energy (W/m2) calculated within 350-1100 nm for two types of mussels (eroded vs uneroded):

astmg173 <- read.csv(file.path(path, "astmg173.csv"), header=T) # ASTM G-173 standard irradiance spectrum for dry air derived from SMARTS v. 2.9.2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0038-092X(01)00054-8)

absorbed_uneroded <- 589.14
absorbed_eroded <- 532.98

minWL <- 350
maxWL <- 1100

totalsolarenergy_WL <- sum(astmg173[which(astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]>=minWL & astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]<=maxWL),"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]) # solar irradiance within the specified range of wavelengths

REFL_uneroded <- 1-(absorbed_uneroded/totalsolarenergy_WL) # =0.1879011
REFL_eroded <- 1-(absorbed_eroded/totalsolarenergy_WL) # =0.2653147

### 2. calculation of REFL using reflectance spectra within 350-1100 nm:

reflectance_uneroded # reflectance values (0-1) extracted from Fig 4A
reflectance_eroded # reflectance values (0-1) extracted from Fig 4A
solarirradiance # ASTM G-173 direct solar irradiance (W/m2/nm) at the wavelengths that match those of reflectance_uneroded  and reflectance_eroded 

REFL_uneroded <- sum(reflectance_uneroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance) # =0.1611066
REFL_eroded <- sum(reflectance_eroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance) # =0.2459432

I guess the small difference in reflectivity values between both methods is due to the fact that the authors used the solar irradiance spectrum measured at their location. I would rather go for the second method so I don't mix different sources of irradiance data. What do you think?

Thanks again for your help!

Best,

Jonathan


​

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
parts:
Hi Jonathan,

That looks good. The difference between methods would indeed be affected by the different irradiance spectra used but it could also be due to differences in the wavelength bands between the observed and predicted values, so that when you sum the energy across a given range you've got different accuracies of integration. You could use R's approxfun method to generate a spline function of the observed solar irradiance vs. wavelength and then use that to get the predicted irradiances at exactly those wavelengths for which you have data. Also, as Warren Porter pointed out, there is a lot of energy in the 1100 to 2600 nm region and you're implicitly assuming that what happens out in that range is similar to what happens in the 350-1100 range.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
parts:
Hi Mike,

Great thanks! Yes I know there is a lot of energy beyond 1100 nm but unfortunately we won’t have the possibility to make those measurements… So I’ll have to stick with the data from Gehman & Harley (2019) and discuss the point. I calculated that 18.27% of the solar irradiance is not accounted for when having data within 350-1100 nm.

Regarding the interpolation of data, I already used smooth.spline() to smooth reflectance data (previously digitized with WebPlotDigitizer) so that they match the wavelengths in the ASTM G-173 irradiance dataset (i.e., every 0.5 nm between 350-400 nm and every 1 nm beyond). Do you suggest I try to get an even finer resolution? Here is the full code and the data if you want to have a look.

path <- "YOURPATH"

astmg173 <- read.csv(file.path(path, "astmg173.csv"), header=T) # ASTM G-173 standard irradiance spectrum for dry air derived from SMARTS v. 2.9.2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0038-092X(01)00054-8)

minWL <- 350
maxWL <- 1100

totalsolarenergy_inf <- sum(astmg173[,"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]) # total solar irradiance
totalsolarenergy_WL <- sum(astmg173[which(astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]>=minWL & astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]<=maxWL),"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]) # solar irradiance within the specified range of wavelengths
solarenergyleft <- 1-(totalsolarenergy_WL/totalsolarenergy_inf) # proportion of the total solar irradiance not accounted for

uneroded <- read.csv(file.path(path, "Gehman&Harley2019Fig4A_Uneroded.csv"), header=F)
eroded <- read.csv(file.path(path, "Gehman&Harley2019Fig4A_Eroded.csv"), header=F)
colnames(uneroded) <- c("wavelength", "reflectivity")
colnames(eroded) <- c("wavelength", "reflectivity")

plot(uneroded$wavelength, uneroded$reflectivity, ylim=c(0, 0.7), xlim=c(300, 1200), pch=19, col="black")
points(eroded$wavelength, eroded$reflectivity, pch=19, col="grey")

xl <- astmg173[which(astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]>=minWL & astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]<=maxWL), "Wvlgth.nm"]

mussel_reflectance <- data.frame(wavelength=xl, eroded=NA, uneroded=NA)

dta <- uneroded

sp <- smooth.spline(dta$wavelength, dta$reflectivity)
sp.pred <- data.frame(x=xl, y=predict(sp, xl)[["y"]])
lines(sp.pred$x, sp.pred$y, col="red")

mussel_reflectance$uneroded <- sp.pred$y

dta <- eroded

sp <- smooth.spline(dta$wavelength, dta$reflectivity)
sp.pred <- data.frame(x=xl, y=predict(sp, xl)[["y"]])
lines(sp.pred$x, sp.pred$y, col="red")

mussel_reflectance$eroded <- sp.pred$y

mussel_reflectance <- cbind(mussel_reflectance, data.frame(solar=astmg173[match(mussel_reflectance$wavelength, astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]),"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]))

solarirradiance <- mussel_reflectance$solar

REFL_uneroded <- sum(mussel_reflectance$uneroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance)
REFL_eroded <- sum(mussel_reflectance$eroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance)

REFL_uneroded # =0.1611066
REFL_eroded # =0.2459432

Best,

Jonathan

​
